title: Indexes and B-trees
summary: Why a query on 20,000 rows can read 40 of them, and how to ask SQLite what it plans to do.

steps.title: The 30-second dashboard
body: Month eight. Avalon Spokes has grown: **20,000 rides** and counting. Teodor's dashboard now takes 30 seconds to load, and he's asking whether he needs a bigger server. Rosa: *"He needs an index."*
Without an index, `SELECT * FROM rides WHERE rider_id = 42` has one option: a **full table scan**. Read all 20,000 rows, keep the 40 that match.
An **index** is a separate, sorted structure (a **B-tree**) that maps a column's values to the rows that have them:

Finding 42 takes a handful of steps down the tree, not 20,000 comparisons: a B-tree over a million rows is only about 3 or 4 levels deep. It's the index at the back of a book, instead of reading every page.

steps.prompt: A table has 1,000,000 rows. Roughly how many rows does a full table scan read to find one rider's 20 rides?
options: It depends on the ORDER BY
steps.explain: A scan can't know where the matches are, so it reads everything. An index finds them in a few page reads plus the 20 rows.

steps.title: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
body: Don't guess whether an index is used. Ask:
- **SEARCH ... USING INDEX** = jump into the index, read only matches.
Other databases: PostgreSQL `EXPLAIN` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to actually run and time it), SQL Server's *Display Estimated Execution Plan* or `SET SHOWPLAN_TEXT ON`, MySQL `EXPLAIN`.

steps.title: Ask for the plan
prompt: Ask SQLite how it would run exactly this query (don't change it):
SELECT id, minutes FROM rides WHERE rider_id = 42;
Tables: `stations(id, name, district)` (40 rows) and `rides(id, rider_id, station_id, started, minutes, fare_cents)` (20,000 rows; `started` is text like `'2026-03-14 08:05:00'`).
solution: SELECT id, minutes FROM rides WHERE rider_id = 42;
setup: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
CREATE TABLE stations (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, district TEXT NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 40) INSERT INTO stations SELECT i, 'Station ' || i, CASE i % 4 WHEN 0 THEN 'Docklands' WHEN 1 THEN 'Old Town' WHEN 2 THEN 'Northside' ELSE 'Harbourside' END FROM n;

CREATE TABLE rides (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, rider_id INTEGER NOT NULL, station_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES stations(id), started TEXT NOT NULL, minutes INTEGER NOT NULL, fare_cents INTEGER NOT NULL);

WITH RECURSIVE n(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i + 1 FROM n WHERE i < 20000) INSERT INTO rides SELECT i, (i * 7919) % 500 + 1, (i * 31) % 40 + 1, datetime('2026-01-01', '+' || ((i * 7) % 300) || ' days', '+' || ((i * 13) % 1440) || ' minutes'), (i * 37) % 55 + 2, ((i * 37) % 55 + 2) * 15 FROM n;
hints: Put `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` in front of the query.
steps.explain: `SCAN rides`: no index on rider_id yet, so all 20,000 rows are read.

steps.prompt: Would an index on `rides (rider_id)` help this query?
steps.explain: An index on rider_id helps conditions on rider_id itself. Wrapping the column in arithmetic hides it from the index (lesson 4).

steps.title: Unique indexes and primary keys
body: Some indexes you get for free:
- `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` in SQLite *is* the table's B-tree (the rowid), so `WHERE id = 7` is always a search.
- Every `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE` constraint creates an index behind the scenes to enforce itself.
`CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` both speeds up lookups and enforces uniqueness:
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX stations_name ON stations (name);
Foreign key columns are **not** indexed automatically in SQLite, PostgreSQL or SQL Server (MySQL's InnoDB does it for you). Joins on `rides.station_id` will want one.

steps.prompt: Which of these lookups already has an index without you creating one?
options: `WHERE stations.id = 7` (id is the INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

steps.title: Index the foreign key
prompt: Riders' history pages are fast now, but station pages (`WHERE station_id = ?`) still scan. Create an index **`rides_station`** on **`rides (station_id)`**, and a **unique** index **`stations_name`** on **`stations (name)`**.
Tables: `stations(id, name, district)` (40 rows) and `rides(id, rider_id, station_id, started, minutes, fare_cents)` (20,000 rows; `started` is text like `'2026-03-14 08:05:00'`).
steps.starter: -- Write your CREATE INDEX statements below
solution: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX stations_name ON stations (name);
